title: Measurement and Analysis of Cancer Biomarkers Using Electrochemical Biosensors: Principles, Platforms, and Clinical Translation

subsections.section_title: Cancer Biomarkers and Their Analytical Significance in Electrochemical Biosensing
subsections.content:
Cancer biomarkers are commonly classified by molecular nature and by the biological process they report. Protein biomarkers remain the most established clinical class and include oncofetal antigens, glycoproteins, enzymes, and receptor fragments such as carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), prostate-specific antigen (PSA), cancer antigen 125 (CA125), and HER2 extracellular domain, which are routinely used in screening adjuncts, prognosis, or treatment monitoring in selected cancers ref [1], ref [2]. Nucleic-acid biomarkers form a second major class, spanning somatic mutations, DNA methylation patterns, messenger RNAs, and non-coding RNAs such as microRNAs; these can capture tumor-specific genomic and epigenomic alterations with greater mechanistic specificity than many circulating proteins ref [3], ref [4].

A complementary classification is based on source and release pathway. Tissue biomarkers are measured directly in tumor specimens, whereas circulating biomarkers are detected in blood and other accessible fluids as soluble factors, circulating tumor cells, extracellular vesicles, or cell-free tumor nucleic acids. The emergence of liquid biopsy has made this distinction analytically important because ctDNA, exosomal cargo, and rare tumor cells provide minimally invasive access to tumor burden, clonal evolution, and resistance mechanisms ref [5], ref [6]. Metabolites and altered glycoforms represent additional classes that reflect cancer-associated reprogramming but often require high selectivity because of matrix complexity and overlap with non-malignant disease ref [7].

From a biosensing perspective, biomarker classes also differ in abundance, stability, and multiplexing needs. High-abundance serum proteins may support direct immunosensing, whereas ultralow-abundance ctDNA, microRNAs, or exosome-associated markers demand amplification strategies and stringent discrimination against closely related sequences or non-tumor vesicles ref [4], ref [6], ref [8]. This classification framework is therefore not merely biological; it directly determines transducer design, recognition chemistry, and the analytical figures of merit required for electrochemical cancer diagnostics.

subsections.section_title: Cancer Biomarkers and Their Analytical Significance in Electrochemical Biosensing
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical roles of biomarkers in cancer management
subsections.content:
In oncology, biomarkers support the continuum from risk stratification and early detection to prognosis, treatment selection, and longitudinal surveillance. Classical serum markers such as prostate-specific antigen and CA125 illustrate both the value and limitations of single-analyte testing: they can enable earlier clinical workup or disease monitoring, but imperfect specificity may also lead to overdiagnosis or unnecessary intervention ref [9], ref [10]. These clinical trade-offs define why biosensing platforms must deliver not only high sensitivity but also context-appropriate selectivity and reproducibility.

Biomarkers also guide therapeutic decisions by identifying actionable molecular alterations and predicting drug response. The clinical implementation of HER2 testing transformed the management of breast cancer by selecting patients for trastuzumab-based therapy, while activating EGFR mutations in non-small-cell lung cancer predict benefit from EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors ref [11], ref [12]. More recently, broad molecular profiling has expanded biomarker-guided treatment across tumor types, linking genomic signatures to targeted agents and immunotherapies in precision oncology ref [13].

For prognosis and disease monitoring, biomarkers are used to estimate recurrence risk, assess residual disease, and track treatment efficacy over time. Multigene expression assays such as the 21-gene recurrence score in breast cancer refine adjuvant therapy decisions beyond conventional clinicopathologic factors ref [14]. In parallel, circulating tumor DNA has emerged as a dynamic biomarker for detecting minimal residual disease and relapse earlier than radiologic progression, highlighting the need for ultrasensitive analytical tools suitable for repeated measurements in liquid biopsy samples ref [15], ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Cancer Biomarkers and Their Analytical Significance in Electrochemical Biosensing
subsections.content:
Cancer biomarkers can be measured in diverse biological matrices, and matrix choice strongly determines clinical utility, attainable sensitivity, and biosensor design. Serum and plasma remain the dominant media for established protein markers because they are routinely collected and supported by standardized clinical workflows; however, abundant background proteins, heterophilic antibodies, and variable anticoagulants can distort electrochemical readout and recognition events. Reviews of circulating tumor markers and blood-based cancer diagnostics emphasize that preanalytical handling, hemolysis, and matrix effects are major determinants of assay reliability ref [17], ref [18].

Urine, saliva, and other noninvasive fluids are increasingly attractive because sampling is simple and repeatable, enabling longitudinal monitoring. Urinary proteins and nucleic acids are especially relevant for urologic malignancies, while saliva has been investigated for oral, lung, and systemic cancers through proteomic and transcriptomic signatures ref [19], ref [20]. Yet these matrices usually contain lower biomarker concentrations than blood and exhibit substantial variability in pH, ionic strength, microbial content, and hydration status, all of which can influence electrode fouling and signal stability.

Liquid biopsy has broadened the matrix landscape to include whole blood fractions enriched for circulating tumor cells, circulating tumor DNA, exosomes, and tumor-educated platelets. These analytes may better reflect tumor heterogeneity and treatment response than single soluble proteins, but they also demand careful isolation and ultrasensitive detection because of extreme rarity and fragmentation ref [21], ref [22], ref [23], ref [24]. For electrochemical biosensing, the selected matrix therefore dictates not only the target class and expected abundance, but also requirements for sample preparation, antifouling interfaces, calibration strategy, and clinical translation.

subsections.section_title: Cancer Biomarkers and Their Analytical Significance in Electrochemical Biosensing
subsections.content:
For cancer biomarker analysis, analytical performance is dictated by the clinical context rather than by signal amplification alone. Early-stage disease often presents biomarkers at very low concentrations and across wide dynamic ranges, so electrochemical biosensors must achieve low limits of detection, broad linearity, and high precision while preserving selectivity in complex media. General analytical guidance for biomarker assays further emphasizes accuracy, calibration traceability, reproducibility, and robustness as prerequisites for clinical translation rather than only proof-of-concept sensitivity ref [25], ref [26].

Specificity is especially critical because many established cancer markers lack disease exclusivity and can be elevated in benign inflammation or organ dysfunction. Consequently, the sensing interface must discriminate target analytes from structurally related proteins, nonspecific adsorption, electroactive interferents, and matrix effects arising from serum, plasma, urine, or saliva. The broader biomarker literature has repeatedly stressed that inadequate selectivity and poor standardization are major causes of irreproducible performance and limited clinical utility ref [27], ref [28].

From a translational perspective, electrochemical platforms should also support multiplexing, rapid turnaround, low sample volume, and reliable operation near clinically relevant decision thresholds. These requirements are particularly important because contemporary oncology increasingly relies on panels of proteins, nucleic acids, and extracellular-vesicle-associated markers rather than single-analyte readouts ref [29], ref [30]. Finally, for blood-based biomarkers such as circulating tumor DNA, assays must combine ultrasensitive detection with stringent control of false positives, preanalytical variability, and inter-assay harmonization to enable longitudinal monitoring and recurrence surveillance ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Cancer Biomarkers and Their Analytical Significance in Electrochemical Biosensing
subsections.content:
Cancer biomarker measurement is challenged first by biology: many clinically relevant analytes occur at very low abundance, display marked interpatient heterogeneity, and fluctuate with tumor burden, treatment, and comorbid inflammation. This is especially problematic in blood, where tumor-derived proteins or nucleic acids are heavily diluted by abundant background species and where benign conditions can elevate canonical markers, reducing diagnostic specificity. Reviews of circulating tumor DNA and blood-based cancer biomarkers have emphasized that rarity, shedding variability, and overlap with nonmalignant processes complicate reliable interpretation and demand highly sensitive yet selective assays ref [31], ref [32].

A second challenge is matrix complexity and preanalytical variability. Serum, plasma, saliva, urine, and other fluids differ in pH, ionic strength, protein content, and fouling propensity, all of which affect capture efficiency and signal transduction. Sample collection tube, clotting time, storage, freeze-thaw cycles, and hemolysis can alter measured concentrations, while biomarker instability or adsorption losses further degrade accuracy. These issues are well documented for circulating nucleic acids and proteins and remain major barriers to assay standardization and interlaboratory reproducibility ref [33], ref [34].

Analytically, cancer management increasingly requires multiplexed measurement rather than reliance on a single marker, because most solitary biomarkers lack sufficient sensitivity or specificity for screening or recurrence surveillance. However, multiplexing introduces cross-reactivity, calibration complexity, and wider dynamic-range requirements, particularly when combining abundant host proteins with ultra-rare tumor signals. Consequently, clinically useful electrochemical biosensors must address fouling, nonspecific adsorption, lot-to-lot variability, and rigorous validation against reference methods under real-world conditions ref [35], ref [36], ref [37].

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Principles and Architectures of Electrochemical Biosensors for Cancer Biomarker Detection
subsections.content:
Electrochemical biosensors for cancer biomarker detection are built from three tightly coupled elements: a biorecognition layer, an electrochemical transducer, and a signal-processing/readout module. The recognition element confers molecular selectivity and may comprise antibodies, nucleic acids, aptamers, peptides, or molecularly imprinted interfaces, depending on whether the target is a protein marker, circulating nucleic acid, exosome-associated ligand, or small metabolite. The transducer converts target binding into changes in current, potential, impedance, or charge-transfer behavior at an electrode/electrolyte interface, while the instrumentation resolves these perturbations under controlled excitation conditions ref [38], ref [39].

Electrode materials and surface chemistry are therefore foundational components rather than passive supports. Gold, carbon, graphene-derived films, conductive polymers, and nanostructured composites are widely used because they provide high surface area, favorable electron-transfer kinetics, and established functionalization routes for immobilizing capture probes with controlled orientation and density ref [40], ref [41]. In cancer biosensing, these interfacial properties are especially important because clinically relevant biomarkers often occur at very low abundance in complex matrices such as serum or plasma; minimizing nonspecific adsorption and preserving probe activity are thus central design requirements ref [42], ref [43].

A complete biosensor architecture also includes redox mediators or reporter species when amplification is needed, antifouling or blocking layers to stabilize performance in biological fluids, and packaging elements such as microfluidic sample handling and miniaturized potentiostats for point-of-care deployment. These components collectively determine sensitivity, selectivity, dynamic range, and practical usability. The emphasis on modular integration—recognition chemistry, engineered electrode interface, and portable electronics—has been a recurring theme in the translation of electrochemical biosensors from laboratory demonstrations toward clinically relevant cancer diagnostics ref [39], ref [44], ref [45].

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Principles and Architectures of Electrochemical Biosensors for Cancer Biomarker Detection
subsections.content:
Electrochemical transduction converts biorecognition at an electrode interface into changes in current, potential, impedance, or charge-transfer kinetics. In cancer biomarker sensing, the most widely used modes are amperometric/voltammetric, potentiometric, conductometric, and impedimetric measurements, each probing a different consequence of target binding. The underlying signal may arise from direct electroactivity of the analyte, catalytic turnover of an enzymatic or nanozyme label, or target-induced modulation of interfacial electron transfer within a redox probe-containing electrolyte ref [38], ref [39].

Amperometric and voltammetric schemes are favored when high sensitivity is required, because faradaic currents can be amplified through enzyme-mediated electrocatalysis or nanomaterial-assisted electron transfer. Differential pulse voltammetry and square-wave voltammetry are especially common for protein and nucleic-acid cancer biomarkers because pulsed methods suppress capacitive background and improve detection at low abundance ref [46], ref [47]. By contrast, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) offers a label-free route: antigen binding, aptamer folding, or hybridization changes the interfacial resistance and double-layer capacitance, enabling quantification without secondary reagents ref [48], ref [49].

The choice of transduction mechanism is therefore a design decision that balances sensitivity, assay complexity, and matrix tolerance. Potentiometric and field-effect approaches can provide rapid equilibrium readout, but many oncological platforms still rely on faradaic or impedimetric transduction because these are readily integrated with affinity layers, redox mediators, and microfabricated electrodes. In practice, successful cancer biosensors often couple a selective capture interface with a transduction mode that maximizes perturbation of the electrode/electrolyte interface while minimizing nonspecific background in serum or whole-blood samples ref [39], ref [50], ref [51].

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Principles and Architectures of Electrochemical Biosensors for Cancer Biomarker Detection
subsections.content:
Electrochemical cancer biosensors are commonly divided into label-free and labeled formats according to whether signal generation arises directly from target binding or from an auxiliary reporter. In label-free schemes, recognition of a biomarker at the electrode interface perturbs interfacial charge transfer, capacitance, or conductivity, which is then read by techniques such as electrochemical impedance spectroscopy or voltammetry. This configuration simplifies assay design, reduces reagent burden, and can better preserve native binding equilibria, making it attractive for real-time and multiplexed analyses of proteins, nucleic acids, and extracellular vesicles ref [52], ref [49]. However, because the readout depends strongly on surface organization and nonspecific adsorption, label-free sensors often face greater susceptibility to matrix effects and limited signal amplification at ultralow analyte levels ref [53].

Labeled strategies introduce electroactive tags, enzymes, nanoparticles, or redox mediators to convert recognition into amplified current or potential changes. Sandwich immunoassays employing enzyme labels remain a dominant approach because they couple high molecular specificity with catalytic amplification, while nanomaterial labels can further increase sensitivity through large payload delivery or electrocatalytic enhancement ref [54], ref [50]. For nucleic acid biomarkers, labeled assays also support target recycling and hybridization chain amplification, improving detection of rare circulating sequences relevant to oncology ref [55].

The choice between the two approaches is therefore application dependent. Label-free detection is advantageous when rapid workflow, minimal processing, and dynamic monitoring are prioritized, whereas labeled formats are generally preferred for early cancer diagnostics demanding sub-picomolar sensitivity and high analytical confidence in complex clinical samples ref [56], ref [57]. Increasingly, hybrid architectures combine label-free interfacial sensing with secondary labeling or nanocatalytic amplification to balance simplicity and performance.

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Principles and Architectures of Electrochemical Biosensors for Cancer Biomarker Detection
subsections.content:
Sensor interface engineering determines how efficiently a cancer biomarker recognition event is converted into an electrochemical perturbation. The interface must simultaneously provide a high density of active binding sites, suppress nonspecific adsorption from complex clinical matrices, and preserve rapid electron transfer. Self-assembled monolayers on gold remain a foundational strategy because thiolated capture probes can be organized with molecular-level control; mixed monolayers using short hydroxyl- or carboxyl-terminated alkanethiols are especially important for tuning probe spacing and reducing fouling, as established in interfacial studies of DNA and protein biosensing ref [58], ref [59].

To increase sensitivity, nanostructured electrodes are widely integrated into the sensing layer. Gold nanoparticles, carbon nanotubes, graphene derivatives, and related hybrid films enlarge electroactive area, improve conductivity, and create favorable microenvironments for immobilized antibodies or aptamers. Such materials have been repeatedly shown to enhance heterogeneous electron transfer and loading of biorecognition elements, including in CNT- and graphene-enabled electrochemical biosensors relevant to ultrasensitive biomarker analysis ref [60], ref [61], ref [50]. Conducting polymers and electropolymerized films add another level of control by allowing thickness-tunable, redox-active, or antifouling coatings that can be deposited directly on microelectrodes under mild conditions ref [62].

For cancer diagnostics, interface engineering is increasingly guided by the demands of serum and whole-blood analysis. Antifouling chemistries based on polyethylene glycol, zwitterionic layers, or bovine serum albumin backfilling are used to stabilize baseline currents and retain selectivity in multiplexed formats. Equally important is oriented immobilization—through protein A/G, streptavidin-biotin coupling, or site-specific aptamer anchoring—which improves accessibility of epitopes and lowers steric hindrance. These design rules are central to modern electrochemical cancer biosensors because clinical performance depends less on the nominal transducer than on how the biointerface manages mass transport, background adsorption, and signal reproducibility ref [59], ref [63], ref [64].

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Principles and Architectures of Electrochemical Biosensors for Cancer Biomarker Detection
subsections.content:
Assay format strongly shapes the analytical performance of electrochemical cancer biosensors. Direct or noncompetitive formats are favored for abundant protein biomarkers because target binding at the electrode can be read as changes in faradaic current, impedance, or capacitance with minimal handling. In contrast, low-abundance analytes often require sandwich configurations in which a capture probe immobilized on the electrode is combined with a secondary labeled antibody or aptamer to amplify signal and improve selectivity; this design has been widely adopted for carcinoembryonic antigen, prostate-specific antigen, and related tumor markers ref [65], ref [43]. Competitive assays remain important for small molecules or short epitopes having only one accessible binding site, although they are less common in mainstream cancer protein analysis.

Detection configuration is equally important. Conventional three-electrode cells remain the benchmark for mechanistic studies, but screen-printed and microfabricated electrodes enable disposable, low-volume assays compatible with point-of-care oncology testing. Multiplexed array layouts are particularly attractive because clinically useful cancer diagnosis often depends on panels rather than single biomarkers; electrochemical microarrays and barcode-style electrode sets have been used to quantify multiple proteins in serum with distinct redox labels or spatially separated sensing sites ref [66], ref [67]. Integration with magnetic beads further decouples target capture from signal readout, allowing preconcentration, reduced matrix fouling, and efficient automation in sandwich immunoassays ref [68].

Recent configurations increasingly combine electrochemical readout with microfluidics and nucleic-acid amplification to support circulating tumor nucleic acid analysis. In these systems, assay architecture is designed not only for sensitivity, but also for sample partitioning, washing efficiency, and compatibility with minimally invasive specimens such as whole blood or serum. Such trends reflect a broader shift from single-step benchtop measurements toward integrated sample-to-answer platforms for multiplexed and ultrasensitive cancer biomarker detection ref [69], ref [70].

subsections.section_title: Materials and Biorecognition Strategies Enabling High-Performance Electrochemical Cancer Biosensors
subsections.content:
Electrode materials determine electron-transfer kinetics, electroactive surface area, and the density of accessible binding sites, making them a primary lever in electrochemical cancer biosensor design. Classical noble-metal electrodes remain important because Au supports well-defined thiol chemistry and stable biofunctional layers, while carbon-based electrodes offer wide potential windows and low background currents. The rise of nanostructured carbon, especially graphene and carbon nanotubes, has been particularly influential because these materials combine high conductivity with large interfacial area and facile integration into label-free and sandwich-type sensing architectures for tumor markers ref [71], ref [60].

Nanostructuring the transducer interface improves sensitivity not only by enlarging surface area but also by reshaping local mass transport and charge-transfer pathways. Hierarchical electrodes based on graphene, nanotubes, metal nanoparticles, and porous metallic frameworks can accelerate heterogeneous electron transfer and create multivalent platforms for immobilizing antibodies or nucleic-acid probes. Gold nanoparticle-modified electrodes are especially widely used in cancer biosensing because they enhance conductivity and permit dense, oriented bioconjugation through Au-thiol interactions ref [72], ref [73]. Likewise, nanoporous gold provides a bicontinuous, high-curvature network that increases loading capacity and preserves electrochemical accessibility in miniaturized devices ref [74].

Recent work also emphasizes hybrid interfaces that couple conductive nanomaterials with robust supports such as screen-printed carbon, indium tin oxide, or metallic microelectrodes to balance analytical performance with manufacturability. Reviews of electrochemical cancer biosensors consistently show that rational control over roughness, porosity, and surface chemistry is central to lowering detection limits for clinically relevant biomarkers, including PSA, CEA, and nucleic-acid signatures ref [51], ref [75]. More broadly, engineered nanointerfaces are valuable because they transform the electrode from a passive conductor into an active recognition-supporting microenvironment ref [76].

subsections.section_title: Materials and Biorecognition Strategies Enabling High-Performance Electrochemical Cancer Biosensors
subsections.content:
Biorecognition elements determine the selectivity of electrochemical cancer biosensors by converting complex molecular differences among proteins, nucleic acids, cells, and extracellular vesicles into measurable interfacial events. Antibodies remain the dominant capture probes for clinically established markers because of their high affinity and compatibility with sandwich and competitive assay formats. For example, prostate-specific antigen and carcinoembryonic antigen have been repeatedly targeted using antibody-functionalized electrodes, illustrating how immunosensing architectures support low detection limits while preserving clinical relevance ref [77], ref [78]. Nonetheless, antibody orientation, batch-to-batch variability, and loss of activity after immobilization continue to motivate alternative receptors.

Aptamers provide a particularly attractive substitute because they are chemically synthesized, readily modified, and can undergo target-induced conformational switching that directly modulates electron transfer. Their utility has been demonstrated for canonical cancer markers such as mucin 1 and other cell-surface or soluble targets, enabling reagentless or signal-amplified electrochemical readout with improved stability relative to proteins ref [79], ref [80]. Nucleic-acid recognition is also central for circulating tumor DNA and microRNA analysis, where complementary probes, molecular beacons, and peptide nucleic acids offer sequence-level discrimination, including single-base mismatch sensitivity that is essential for mutation-informed oncology assays ref [81].

Beyond antibodies and aptamers, engineered affinity scaffolds broaden the capture toolbox. Lectins exploit altered glycosylation in malignant transformation, enabling recognition of cancer-associated glycophenotypes without requiring a specific protein epitope ref [82]. Peptides and small binding proteins, including affibodies, can further improve receptor density and mass transport because of their small size and robust folding; HER2-targeting affibody reagents exemplify this strategy for compact and stable recognition interfaces ref [83]. More recently, extracellular-vesicle sensing has benefited from membrane-protein-directed capture chemistries tailored to nanoscale vesicles, underscoring that optimal biorecognition now depends not only on affinity, but also on target size, epitope accessibility, and compatibility with miniaturized electrochemical transduction ref [84].

subsections.section_title: Materials and Biorecognition Strategies Enabling High-Performance Electrochemical Cancer Biosensors
subsections.content:
Nanomaterial-assisted amplification is central to electrochemical cancer biosensing because it increases effective electrode area, accelerates electron transfer, and enables high-density loading of redox tags, enzymes, or capture probes. Gold nanoparticles were among the earliest and most influential platforms, providing conductive, biocompatible scaffolds for immobilizing biomolecules while also supporting catalytic or stripping-based readout schemes for ultrasensitive biomarker detection ref [85]. Carbon nanomaterials, especially carbon nanotubes and graphene derivatives, further improved sensitivity by combining large surface area with favorable charge-transport properties and facile integration into composite electrodes ref [60], ref [71].

A major advance has been the use of engineered nanostructures as multifunctional labels rather than passive supports. Semiconductor and metallic nanoparticles can encode electroactive signatures for multiplexed assays, whereas mesoporous silica, dendritic Au, and hybrid nanocomposites can carry large numbers of signal molecules or secondary recognition elements. This principle is exemplified by nanoporous and metal-enhanced barcodes for parallel protein analysis, as well as by nanoceria- and noble-metal-based catalytic labels that amplify current without the instability of natural enzymes ref [86], ref [87]. Such strategies are especially attractive for low-abundance cancer biomarkers, where signal gain must be achieved without sacrificing specificity.

More recently, two-dimensional and framework materials have broadened the amplification toolbox. MXenes offer metallic conductivity and abundant surface terminations for probe conjugation, while metal-organic frameworks and related porous hybrids provide exceptionally high cargo capacity for electroactive mediators and catalytic centers ref [88], ref [89]. Nonetheless, amplification performance depends not only on intrinsic material properties but also on colloidal stability, batch reproducibility, and resistance to nonspecific adsorption in complex clinical matrices. Consequently, successful designs increasingly pair nanomaterial amplification with controlled interface chemistry and antifouling layers to translate analytical gains into robust cancer diagnostics ref [89], ref [90].

subsections.section_title: Materials and Biorecognition Strategies Enabling High-Performance Electrochemical Cancer Biosensors
subsections.content:
Surface functionalization governs the orientation, density, and long-term activity of capture probes at electrochemical interfaces, and is therefore a central determinant of analytical sensitivity and reproducibility. On gold electrodes, self-assembled alkanethiol monolayers remain the dominant platform because they provide ordered, tailorable interfacial chemistry and enable coupling of antibodies, aptamers, or peptides through terminal carboxyl, amine, or maleimide groups; mixed monolayers are particularly useful for balancing probe loading with accessibility and suppressing nonspecific adsorption ref [1], ref [2]. For carbon and oxide electrodes, aryl diazonium electrografting offers covalent and electrochemically addressable surface modification with high stability under repeated interrogation, although excessive multilayer growth can hinder charge transfer if not carefully controlled ref [3].

Immobilization chemistry must also preserve biorecognition function. Carbodiimide coupling between surface carboxylates and lysine residues is widely used because of its simplicity, but it often yields heterogeneous antibody orientations and variable antigen accessibility. To address this, protein A/G-mediated assembly and site-selective conjugation strategies have been adopted to enrich upright antibody presentation and improve binding efficiency ref [4], ref [5]. For nucleic-acid receptors, thiolated aptamers on gold combined with mercaptohexanol backfilling provide a well-established route to control probe spacing, reduce steric crowding, and stabilize folding-dependent recognition, which is especially important in electrochemical aptasensors operating in serum or whole blood ref [6].

Polymer and bioinspired interlayers further expand immobilization options. Electropolymerized films and polydopamine coatings can conformally functionalize nanostructured electrodes, offering abundant reactive groups for secondary coupling while maintaining compatibility with biomolecules and complex substrates ref [7]. More recently, zwitterionic and oligo(ethylene glycol)-based coatings have been integrated with these chemistries to combine robust probe attachment with low-fouling performance, an important requirement for cancer biomarker detection directly in clinically relevant matrices ref [8]. Overall, effective functionalization is not merely a linking step, but a means of engineering interfacial transport, bioactivity, and resistance to matrix-induced signal loss.

subsections.section_title: Materials and Biorecognition Strategies Enabling High-Performance Electrochemical Cancer Biosensors
subsections.content:
Antifouling and biocompatible interfaces are essential for electrochemical cancer biosensors operating in serum, plasma, saliva, or whole blood, where nonspecific adsorption of proteins, cells, and lipids can mask low-abundance biomarker signals. A central design principle is the creation of highly hydrated interfacial layers that suppress van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions while preserving charge transfer and receptor accessibility. Poly(ethylene glycol)-based coatings were among the earliest broadly adopted strategies for resisting protein adsorption, and self-assembled oligo(ethylene glycol) monolayers established the importance of densely packed, water-rich films for bioinert behavior ref [91], ref [92].

More recently, zwitterionic materials have emerged as particularly effective antifouling platforms because their strong ionic solvation generates tightly bound hydration shells. Reviews of zwitterionic interfaces and low-fouling biomaterials have highlighted sulfobetaine, carboxybetaine, and phosphorylcholine chemistries as robust candidates for biosensor coatings in complex media ref [63], ref [93]. Such coatings can be combined with nanostructured electrodes to maintain high surface area while limiting matrix-induced background, an important balance in cancer biomarker assays that demand both sensitivity and clinical specificity.

Biocompatibility also depends on immobilization chemistry. Mixed monolayers, hydrogels, and polydopamine-derived films can provide anchoring sites for antibodies or aptamers while minimizing denaturation and preserving interfacial hydration. Mussel-inspired polydopamine has proven especially versatile as a universal surface primer for secondary functionalization under mild conditions ref [94]. In parallel, ultralow-fouling poly(carboxybetaine methacrylate) brushes and related surface-grafted polymers have shown excellent resistance to nonspecific adsorption and favorable performance in undiluted biological fluids ref [95], ref [96]. For implantable or continuous-monitoring electrochemical systems, such interfacial engineering is further linked to reduced foreign-body reactions and improved long-term signal stability ref [97].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Measurement and Signal Analysis of Diverse Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.content:
Electrochemical protein biomarker detection has centered on clinically established cancer antigens such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), cancer antigen 125 (CA125), and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), because these targets provide clear benchmarks for evaluating analytical sensitivity, dynamic range, and compatibility with serum matrices. Early work established sandwich immunoassays on electrode surfaces as a dominant format, combining capture antibodies with enzyme or nanoparticle labels to amplify faradaic readout and push detection into the pg mL−1 regime for PSA and related markers ref [98], ref [99]. Subsequent studies showed that nanostructured interfaces, including carbon nanotube forests and metallic nanoparticle-modified electrodes, increase effective surface area and accelerate electron transfer, thereby improving both loading of affinity probes and signal gain ref [100], ref [101].

A major trend has been the migration from conventional antibodies toward aptamers and hybrid recognition schemes to improve stability, regeneration, and integration into miniaturized devices. Aptamer-based electrochemical sensors for cancer proteins such as MUC1 demonstrated that conformational switching can directly modulate current or impedance without requiring extensive washing steps, enabling simpler assay architectures ref [102]. In parallel, label-free electrochemical impedance spectroscopy has been widely adopted for protein sensing because binding-induced changes in interfacial resistance can be quantified without secondary reagents, although nonspecific adsorption and matrix effects remain important limitations in complex clinical samples ref [103].

For translational use, the main challenge is not only achieving ultralow limits of detection but also preserving selectivity, calibration robustness, and reproducibility across heterogeneous patient specimens. Reviews of cancer biosensing consistently emphasize that multiplexed protein panels, antifouling surface chemistries, and rigorous validation against standard immunoassays are essential if electrochemical platforms are to move from proof-of-concept demonstrations toward routine clinical decision support ref [51], ref [104].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Measurement and Signal Analysis of Diverse Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.content:
Nucleic acid biomarkers—including circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), microRNAs, messenger RNAs, and aberrantly methylated sequences—are attractive electrochemical targets because they directly report tumor genotype and can often be measured in minimally invasive samples. Electrochemical nucleic acid assays typically exploit sequence-specific hybridization at gold, carbon, or magnetic bead interfaces, with signal generation based on redox labels, electrocatalytic reporters, or impedance changes. Early DNA sensors established the feasibility of highly selective electrical readout of hybridization and mismatch discrimination, while subsequent work translated these concepts to clinically relevant cancer-associated sequences and low-abundance RNA targets using amplified transduction schemes such as chronocoulometry and nanoparticle-assisted signaling ref [105], ref [106], ref [107].

For cancer applications, assay design has increasingly focused on sensitivity under complex matrix conditions and on distinguishing closely related mutant and wild-type sequences. Label-free electrochemical impedance approaches are attractive for simple workflows, whereas sandwich and hairpin formats improve selectivity for short targets such as miRNAs. Integration with enzymatic or catalytic amplification—including nuclease-assisted recycling, rolling-circle amplification, and CRISPR-based collateral cleavage—has further lowered detection limits and expanded multiplexing potential. In particular, electrochemical CRISPR platforms have demonstrated programmable recognition of oncogenic DNA mutations and viral nucleic acids with compact instrumentation, suggesting a route toward point-of-care molecular oncology ref [108], ref [109].

Despite these advances, robust clinical translation requires tighter control of pre-analytical variation, normalization across extraction and amplification steps, and rigorous calibration in the low-copy-number regime characteristic of liquid biopsy samples. Studies of circulating miRNAs and ctDNA have also emphasized the need for orthogonal validation against PCR or sequencing workflows and for panels rather than single analytes to improve diagnostic accuracy. Accordingly, current research is moving toward integrated devices that combine target enrichment, anti-fouling electrode chemistry, and multivariate interpretation of electrochemical outputs for quantitative molecular profiling in real specimens ref [110], ref [111].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Measurement and Signal Analysis of Diverse Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.content:
Exosomes and other small extracellular vesicles (EVs) are attractive electrochemical targets because they are abundant in biofluids and carry membrane proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids that reflect tumor state. Foundational studies established that circulating exosomes transfer functional biomolecules between cells and can serve as accessible cancer biomarkers, motivating assay formats that capture intact vesicles rather than isolated cargoes ref [112], ref [113]. In electrochemical sensing, this has favored immunoaffinity and aptamer-based interfaces targeting canonical tetraspanins (CD9, CD63, CD81) or tumor-associated surface markers such as EpCAM, HER2, and EGFR.

A major design challenge is the nanoscale size and heterogeneity of EVs. Nanostructured electrodes, magnetic bead enrichment, and sandwich architectures are therefore commonly used to amplify binding events and improve mass transport. Early electrochemical platforms demonstrated direct profiling of exosomal proteins from clinical samples, including integrated chips for quantitative exosome analysis and electrokinetic enrichment approaches that improved sensitivity in small volumes ref [114], ref [115]. More recent biosensors combine antifouling interfaces with enzyme, redox-probe, or nanoparticle amplification to detect low-abundance tumor EV subpopulations in serum, while preserving relatively simple instrumentation ref [116], ref [117].

Analytically, EV sensing requires careful normalization because signal can reflect vesicle number, marker density, or both. This has encouraged orthogonal calibration against nanoparticle tracking analysis, electron microscopy, or conventional immunoassays, as well as multiplexed readout of several surface proteins to distinguish disease-associated phenotypes ref [118], ref [119]. For cancer applications, the most clinically relevant direction is likely not single-marker detection alone, but integrated electrochemical phenotyping of EV abundance and composition in minimally processed biofluids.

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Measurement and Signal Analysis of Diverse Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.subsection_title: Cell-based and circulating tumor cell analysis
subsections.content:
Electrochemical analysis of intact cancer cells and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) extends biomarker sensing from soluble targets to whole-cell phenotypes, enabling assessment of surface antigens, viability, adhesion, and metastatic potential. Early work established that impedance-based cytosensors can transduce cell capture and attachment without labels, providing a route to dynamic monitoring of cancer cell behavior on microelectrodes ref [120]. This principle has been adapted to affinity interfaces bearing antibodies or aptamers against epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM), HER2, MUC1, and related markers, so that the presence of rare tumor cells is converted into changes in charge-transfer resistance, capacitance, or redox current ref [121], ref [122].

For CTC analysis, electrochemical platforms are especially attractive because they can be integrated with microfluidics for enrichment from whole blood and then coupled to sensitive readout on the same chip. In this context, capture on nanostructured electrodes or aptamer-modified surfaces improves collision frequency and interfacial area, while enzymatic or nanoparticle labels further amplify the weak signal generated by very low cell counts ref [122], ref [123]. Beyond simple enumeration, electrochemical assays have also been used to profile cell-surface glycans and receptor expression, offering phenotypic discrimination between tumor subtypes and potentially between epithelial and mesenchymal CTC states ref [124], ref [125].

Key analytical challenges remain the rarity and heterogeneity of CTCs, nonspecific adsorption from blood matrices, and the tendency of marker-negative subpopulations to evade capture. Accordingly, recent studies emphasize multiplexed recognition and hybrid isolation-transduction devices rather than reliance on a single epithelial antigen ref [123], ref [126]. Future progress will likely come from integrating electrochemical sensing with image-based validation and downstream molecular analysis, so that cell counting, phenotype assignment, and treatment monitoring can be performed in a unified workflow ref [126], ref [127].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Measurement and Signal Analysis of Diverse Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.content:
Multiplexed electrochemical detection is increasingly important in oncology because single markers rarely capture the heterogeneity of tumor initiation, progression, and treatment response. Electrochemical multiplexing has been implemented through electrode arrays, barcode-like nanolabels, and spatially resolved microfabricated sensing interfaces that allow parallel readout of protein, nucleic acid, or vesicle-associated targets in small sample volumes. Early studies demonstrated simultaneous electrochemical immunodetection of multiple cancer-associated proteins by assigning different capture chemistries to distinct electrodes and decoding the response voltammetrically or amperometrically, thereby improving diagnostic specificity over single-analyte assays ref [128], ref [129].

A major design challenge is preserving analytical separation while maintaining comparable sensitivity across channels. This has motivated the use of redox reporters with distinct formal potentials, quantum-dot or metal-ion labels released after binding events, and nanostructured electrode surfaces that enhance loading density and electron transfer. Such strategies have enabled multi-protein assays for clinically relevant panels including carcinoembryonic antigen, alpha-fetoprotein, prostate-specific antigen, and CA-related markers, often reaching low-abundance detection limits compatible with serum analysis ref [130], ref [131], ref [132]. Microfluidic integration further improves multiplexing by reducing cross-contamination, automating reagent delivery, and supporting point-of-care operation ref [69].

For translation, however, multiplexed platforms must address calibration drift, matrix-dependent cross-reactivity, and the statistical interpretation of correlated biomarker panels. Increasingly, electrochemical arrays are therefore coupled with chemometric or machine-learning workflows to transform multichannel current patterns into clinically actionable signatures rather than isolated concentration values. This systems-level approach is especially attractive for liquid biopsy applications, where combined analysis of proteins, nucleic acids, and extracellular-vesicle markers may outperform any single biomarker class ref [69], ref [51], ref [133].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Measurement and Signal Analysis of Diverse Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.content:
Signal processing is central to converting raw electrochemical readouts into reliable biomarker concentrations, especially when cancer assays operate near background limits or in complex biofluids. For voltammetric methods, baseline drift, capacitive current, and electrode-to-electrode variability are commonly mitigated through smoothing, polynomial baseline subtraction, peak deconvolution, and normalization to internal or ratiometric signals. The practical importance of these steps is evident in square-wave and pulse voltammetric biosensors, where waveform parameters strongly influence faradaic-to-nonfaradaic discrimination and thus analytical sensitivity ref [134]. More broadly, careful treatment of noise and background is essential because apparent low-level signals can otherwise reflect matrix effects rather than true biomarker binding ref [135].

Data interpretation increasingly extends beyond univariate calibration. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, for example, produces multivariate spectra whose diagnostic value depends on equivalent-circuit fitting and model selection; the physical meaning and limitations of such fitting have been extensively discussed, including risks of overparameterization and nonunique solutions ref [136], ref [137]. In cancer biosensing, these issues become more acute in multiplexed or label-free platforms, where partial frequency-domain overlap and interfacial heterogeneity complicate direct extraction of a single resistance or capacitance term.

Machine-learning-assisted analysis is therefore gaining traction for classifying complex electrochemical signatures and integrating multimodal biomarker panels. Foundational chemometric strategies such as principal component analysis and partial least-squares regression remain important for dimensionality reduction and calibration ref [138], while broader machine-learning frameworks have been adopted in biosensor analytics to improve pattern recognition, compensate for sensor drift, and support clinical decision rules ref [139], ref [140]. Nonetheless, robust validation, transparent preprocessing, and external testing on independent cohorts remain critical to avoid optimistic performance estimates and to ensure interpretability in translational cancer diagnostics ref [141].

subsections.section_title: Device Integration, Point-of-Care Platforms, and Translational Applications
subsections.content:
Miniaturized and portable electrochemical platforms have become central to translating cancer biosensors from benchtop prototypes to deployable diagnostic systems. Progress has been driven by the co-development of screen-printed and paper-based electrodes, low-power potentiostats, and smartphone-readable interfaces that reduce instrumentation burden while preserving analytical sensitivity. Reviews of wearable and mobile electrochemical sensors have emphasized how miniaturization changes the design space from purely analytical optimization toward system-level constraints such as power management, wireless communication, sample handling, and calibration robustness ref [142], ref [143]. In parallel, portable electrochemical readers integrated with nanostructured sensing interfaces have shown that compact formats can support clinically relevant detection of cancer-associated proteins and nucleic acids without conventional laboratory infrastructure ref [144], ref [145].

A key engineering trend is the use of disposable microfabricated or printed sensor strips coupled to handheld electronics. Screen-printed electrode platforms, long established as low-cost transducers, remain particularly attractive because they support multiplexing, surface modification with nanomaterials, and scalable manufacturing ref [146]. Paper-based electrochemical devices further extend portability by combining capillary-driven fluid transport with inexpensive substrates and simple visual or electronic readout; these features are especially relevant for decentralized cancer screening and longitudinal monitoring in resource-limited settings ref [147]. More recently, flexible and epidermal electrochemical systems have demonstrated how conformal substrates and integrated electronics can broaden sampling modes beyond standard blood testing toward sweat and interstitial-fluid analysis, although cancer-specific validation remains comparatively early-stage ref [143], ref [148].

Despite these advances, successful deployment depends on balancing miniaturization with assay reliability. Portable systems must maintain stable reference behavior, minimize matrix effects in complex biofluids, and provide reproducible quantitative performance across users and environments. The broader movement toward smartphone-based biosensing illustrates both the opportunity and the challenge: consumer electronics enable connectivity and user-friendly interfaces, but clinically credible cancer diagnostics still require rigorous analytical benchmarking, secure data workflows, and manufacturable cartridge-reader integration ref [145], ref [149].

subsections.section_title: Device Integration, Point-of-Care Platforms, and Translational Applications
subsections.content:
Microfluidic and lab-on-a-chip integration has been central to translating electrochemical cancer biosensors from benchtop assays into compact diagnostic systems. By miniaturizing fluid handling, these platforms reduce sample and reagent consumption, shorten diffusion distances, and enable tighter control over mass transport at the electrode interface, thereby improving assay speed and reproducibility. Early electrochemical microfluidic immunoarrays demonstrated multiplexed protein detection with clinically relevant sensitivity, including devices for oral and prostate cancer biomarkers that combined patterned electrodes, on-chip washing, and automated reagent delivery ref [69], ref [150]. Such architectures established the feasibility of integrating capture, labeling, and electrochemical readout within a single disposable cartridge.

Subsequent work expanded microfluidic integration toward more automated and clinically realistic workflows. Soper and colleagues developed microfluidic chips for immunomagnetic enrichment and electrochemical interrogation of circulating tumor cells, illustrating how cell isolation and sensing can be coupled on-chip for liquid-biopsy applications ref [151]. Parallel advances in centrifugal and valve-based microfluidics have further supported sample preparation and multiplex immunoassays in portable formats ref [152]. Reviews of micro total analysis systems emphasize that the main engineering challenge is not only analytical sensitivity, but also robust integration of plasma separation, mixing, incubation, and fouling-resistant electrochemical interfaces in manufacturable devices ref [153], ref [154].

For translational cancer diagnostics, the value of lab-on-a-chip integration lies in end-to-end workflow simplification. Electrochemical microfluidic devices are particularly attractive because they can be batch-fabricated, readily interfaced with low-power electronics, and adapted to diverse analytes including proteins, nucleic acids, exosomes, and whole cells. However, clinical deployment still depends on reliable handling of complex biospecimens, stable reagent storage, and standardized cartridge-to-reader operation. Recent organ-on-chip and cancer-chip perspectives also suggest that future platforms may combine sensing with functional ex vivo testing, extending microfluidic electrochemistry beyond detection toward therapy guidance ref [155], ref [156].

subsections.section_title: Device Integration, Point-of-Care Platforms, and Translational Applications
subsections.subsection_title: Liquid biopsy and noninvasive cancer monitoring
subsections.content:
Liquid biopsy has become a major translational target for electrochemical biosensing because it enables repeated, minimally invasive sampling of blood and other biofluids to monitor tumor burden, molecular evolution, and treatment response. Clinically informative analytes include circulating tumor cells (CTCs), circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), extracellular vesicles, and tumor-associated proteins, each spanning different abundance ranges and preanalytical constraints. The broader oncology literature established the clinical relevance of CTC enumeration and molecular profiling, as well as the utility of ctDNA for tracking resistance and relapse in solid tumors [1,2]. For electrochemical platforms, these analytes are attractive because they can be coupled to affinity capture, nucleic-acid hybridization, or signal amplification strategies that are inherently compatible with miniaturized electrodes and portable readers.

Among liquid-biopsy targets, CTCs and exosomes have been especially prominent in device-oriented electrochemical studies. The CellSearch system provided an early benchmark for the prognostic value of CTC counts in metastatic breast cancer [3], motivating alternative sensing formats with lower cost and easier decentralization. In parallel, work on exosomal biomarkers showed that tumor-derived vesicles can be profiled from patient serum using integrated microfluidic and electrochemical approaches, including immunocapture and on-chip signal transduction [4,5]. These studies illustrate an important systems trend: noninvasive cancer monitoring increasingly depends on multiplexed, low-volume assays that can process complex biofluids while preserving analytical sensitivity.

For ctDNA, the translational challenge is to detect rare mutant alleles in a high background of wild-type nucleic acids. The clinical significance of this problem was highlighted by studies showing that circulating DNA can reveal acquired resistance, such as EGFR pathway alterations during targeted therapy [2,6]. Electrochemical DNA sensors are therefore moving toward highly selective mutation discrimination, often by integrating isothermal amplification, nanostructured electrodes, or CRISPR-assisted readout with sample-to-answer workflows. More broadly, the roadmap for noninvasive cancer monitoring is shaped by liquid-biopsy standardization efforts emphasizing analytical validation, preanalytical control, and clinically meaningful endpoints [7,8]; these requirements are crucial if electrochemical assays are to progress from promising prototypes to longitudinal monitoring tools in routine oncology.

subsections.section_title: Device Integration, Point-of-Care Platforms, and Translational Applications
subsections.content:
For electrochemical cancer diagnostics to function at the point of care, analytical sensitivity must be balanced against operational simplicity, short turnaround time, and robustness to minimally processed samples. The ASSURED framework remains a useful benchmark for low-resource and decentralized testing, emphasizing affordability, sensitivity, specificity, user-friendliness, rapidity, equipment-free operation, and deliverability ref [163]. In practice, this translates into design choices such as single-step assay workflows, dry-stored reagents, capillary-driven sample handling, and compact potentiostatic readout, while maintaining clinically relevant limits of detection in complex matrices such as whole blood, saliva, or urine.

Usability and implementation constraints are often as limiting as sensor chemistry. Reviews of point-of-care diagnostics have highlighted the importance of calibration stability, quality control, lot-to-lot reproducibility, and resistance to environmental variation, all of which can dominate performance outside laboratory settings ref [164], ref [165]. Smartphone-linked electrochemical systems can reduce instrumentation burden and support data transmission, but they also introduce requirements for secure connectivity, standardized interfaces, and validated software pipelines ref [166]. Human-factors engineering, including minimal operator steps and unambiguous result presentation, is therefore essential for adoption in oncology screening and monitoring pathways.

Finally, translational success depends on demonstrating clinical utility rather than only analytical performance. Comparative studies of established point-of-care platforms, such as the i-STAT system, show that agreement with central laboratory methods, specimen-dependent bias, and workflow integration must all be assessed before routine deployment ref [167], ref [168]. Broader guidance from biosensor translational reviews and WHO target product profile thinking further suggests that cost-per-test, manufacturability, shelf life, and regulatory evidence generation should be considered early in device development rather than after proof-of-concept optimization ref [169], ref [170].

subsections.section_title: Device Integration, Point-of-Care Platforms, and Translational Applications
subsections.content:
Clinical translation of electrochemical cancer biosensors depends less on proof-of-concept sensitivity than on rigorous validation against established clinical comparators. Benchmarking should therefore include analytical agreement with gold-standard methods such as immunohistochemistry, ELISA, PCR, and next-generation sequencing, together with prospective assessment of sensitivity, specificity, reproducibility, and performance across heterogeneous patient cohorts. Reporting standards developed for biomarker studies, including the STARD statement and REMARK guidelines, are particularly relevant because they emphasize transparent cohort definition, reference standards, and handling of indeterminate results ref [171], ref [172].

Comparative studies in liquid biopsy provide a useful model for this process. The FDA approval study of the CellSearch system established that analytically standardized circulating tumor cell enumeration could stratify prognosis in metastatic breast cancer and offered a benchmark for subsequent device-based assays ref [157]. Likewise, concordance studies between blood-based genotyping and tissue testing, such as digital PCR and BEAMing analyses of EGFR or KRAS mutations, illustrate how sensitivity claims must be interpreted relative to allele fraction, tumor burden, and sampling timepoint rather than as absolute device attributes ref [173], ref [174].

For electrochemical platforms, clinically meaningful benchmarking should also include lot-to-lot stability, operator dependence, matrix effects in whole blood or plasma, and decision-threshold calibration under realistic prevalence conditions. Comparative diagnostic accuracy is ideally evaluated in blinded, multi-center cohorts, as emphasized in broader translational reviews of cancer biomarkers and omics-derived signatures ref [175], ref [176]. In practice, the most credible path to adoption is not replacing incumbent assays outright, but demonstrating added value in rapid triage, serial monitoring, or decentralized testing where electrochemical devices offer logistical advantages ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Needs, and Future Directions in Electrochemical Biosensing for Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.content:
Despite major gains in sensitivity, electrochemical biosensors for cancer biomarkers still face fundamental analytical limitations that impede routine clinical deployment. Reported limits of detection are often achieved in buffered media rather than in whole blood, serum, or plasma, where nonspecific adsorption, electrode fouling, and ionic-strength effects distort charge-transfer behavior and increase false responses. These matrix-dependent artifacts are especially problematic for low-abundance protein biomarkers and circulating nucleic acids, whose clinically relevant concentrations overlap with background noise and pre-analytical variability ref [51], ref [177].

Selectivity is also constrained by the dependence on biological recognition layers that can lose affinity after immobilization, exhibit lot-to-lot variability, or cross-react with structurally related analytes. For affinity-based electrochemical assays, signal amplification strategies using nanomaterials, redox labels, or enzymatic cascades may improve apparent sensitivity but can also magnify drift, instability, and calibration complexity, thereby reducing robustness outside controlled laboratory settings ref [43], ref [50]. In multiplexed formats, these issues are compounded by electrical cross-talk, differential surface loading, and nonuniform mass transport across microelectrode arrays ref [178].

A further limitation is the incomplete analytical validation of many published platforms. Important performance characteristics—including inter-assay precision, dynamic range in clinically relevant matrices, interference tolerance, and comparability with gold-standard immunoassays or molecular tests—are often underreported. Recent efforts toward wearable, flexible, and microfluidic electrochemical systems are promising, but they introduce additional constraints related to mechanical reliability, sample handling, and long-term stability that must be resolved before biomarker measurements can be considered clinically actionable ref [179], ref [180].

Overall, the key technical challenge is not merely pushing sensitivity lower, but ensuring that electrochemical responses remain quantitatively accurate, selective, and reproducible in heterogeneous real-world specimens. Future work should therefore prioritize matrix-aware sensor design, anti-fouling interfaces, rigorous interference testing, and analytically validated benchmarking against established clinical methods ref [177], ref [180], ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Needs, and Future Directions in Electrochemical Biosensing for Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.content:
Standardization and reproducibility remain major bottlenecks for translating electrochemical cancer biomarker biosensors from proof-of-concept studies to clinically credible assays. Reported analytical performance is often strongly dependent on electrode pretreatment, nanomaterial synthesis history, bioreceptor immobilization chemistry, and the choice of redox probe, making cross-study comparison difficult. The broader reproducibility concerns identified for nanobiosensors and omics-oriented biomarker assays are directly relevant here: inadequate control of preanalytical variables, poor interlaboratory harmonization, and selective reporting can inflate apparent sensitivity while obscuring robustness ref [181], ref [182]. In electroanalysis specifically, even modest changes in surface roughness, fouling state, or reference electrode stability can shift impedance or voltammetric signals enough to compromise lot-to-lot comparability ref [183].

A practical standardization agenda should therefore include consensus reporting of sample provenance, storage conditions, matrix effects, calibration model, dynamic range, blank definition, and replicate structure, alongside full disclosure of electrode fabrication and surface characterization. Community adoption of minimum information frameworks analogous to the MIRIBEL checklist for bio-nano experiments would improve transparency in biosensor studies ref [184]. Equally important is the use of validated analytical protocols for limit-of-detection estimation and calibration, since inconsistent statistical treatment remains common in sensor papers ref [185]. For cancer biomarker applications, standard reference materials and commutable clinical samples are especially needed to benchmark recovery, selectivity, and agreement with established immunoassays.

Reproducibility must also be demonstrated beyond a single laboratory. Experience from microfluidics and bioanalytical diagnostics shows that device performance often deteriorates when transferred across operators, sites, and manufacturing batches ref [186], ref [187]. Accordingly, future electrochemical biosensor studies should prioritize blinded testing, interlaboratory ring trials, accelerated stability studies, and predefined acceptance criteria for batch release. Alignment with internationally recognized requirements for in vitro diagnostic quality management and method validation will be essential if cancer biomarker sensors are to progress toward regulatory evaluation and routine clinical use ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Needs, and Future Directions in Electrochemical Biosensing for Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.content:
A persistent obstacle to translation of electrochemical cancer-biomarker biosensors is the gap between laboratory fabrication and high-throughput, quality-controlled manufacturing. Many high-performing reports rely on manually assembled nanostructured electrodes, drop-cast recognition layers, or batch-specific surface chemistries that are difficult to reproduce at wafer, roll-to-roll, or cartridge scale. Printed and paper-based electrochemical platforms offer a more manufacturable route because screen-printing, inkjet patterning, and laminated microfluidics can reduce per-test cost and support disposable formats, but lot-to-lot variability in inks, curing, electrode roughness, and biomolecule immobilization still affects analytical drift and shelf life ref [188], ref [189], ref [190].

Scalability also depends on integration rather than sensor performance alone. Commercially viable systems require stable packaging, reagent storage, fluid handling, calibration strategy, and interoperable readout electronics. Experience from glucose test strips shows that success comes from tightly controlled mass manufacture, enzyme/reagent stabilization, and robust electrochemical metering rather than maximal analytical sophistication ref [191]. Analogously, cancer biosensors must transition from proof-of-concept nanomaterials toward design-for-manufacture frameworks, including standardized electrode substrates, automated biofunctionalization, and accelerated aging studies. Microfabrication and multiplexed biochip manufacturing can support this shift, but they demand process control comparable to established in vitro diagnostics ref [38], ref [192].

Future progress will likely come from modular manufacturing strategies that combine printed electrodes with scalable microfluidics and low-cost electronics, as demonstrated in emerging point-of-care electrochemical systems ref [193], ref [194]. For cancer biomarker assays, manufacturability should therefore be treated as a primary design criterion from the outset, with explicit reporting of batch reproducibility, storage stability, and compatibility with automated assembly.

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Needs, and Future Directions in Electrochemical Biosensing for Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.content:
Regulatory translation of electrochemical cancer biosensors depends less on proof-of-concept sensitivity than on demonstrating analytically validated, clinically meaningful performance in intended-use populations. Guidance developed for in vitro diagnostics emphasizes predefined use cases, traceable calibration, lot-to-lot consistency, interference testing, and multicenter evidence of accuracy and precision; these requirements are particularly important because many published biosensors are evaluated only in buffered media or small retrospective cohorts rather than under CLIA-relevant workflows or FDA-aligned validation frameworks ref [195], ref [196].

Clinical adoption also requires showing that a biosensor improves decision-making relative to established laboratory assays, not merely that it correlates with them. The STARD 2015 framework highlights transparent reporting of patient selection, reference standards, indeterminate results, and sources of bias in diagnostic accuracy studies ref [171]. For liquid-biopsy-oriented devices, regulatory expectations are increasingly shaped by experience from circulating tumor DNA and multicancer early detection assays, where assay standardization, specimen handling, and prospective clinical utility studies have emerged as decisive barriers to approval and reimbursement ref [197], ref [198].

Accordingly, viable adoption pathways will likely involve stepwise development: first as laboratory-developed tests or adjunct triage tools in high-prevalence settings, then as fully regulated in vitro diagnostics after prospective validation, health-economic assessment, and manufacturing controls are established. Recent translational reviews of biosensors stress the need for quality-by-design, human-factor engineering for point-of-care deployment, and early engagement with regulators, clinicians, and payers so that device architecture, analyte panel selection, and trial design are aligned from the outset ref [199], ref [200].

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Needs, and Future Directions in Electrochemical Biosensing for Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.content:
Emerging work is shifting electrochemical cancer biosensing from single-analyte, benchtop assays toward integrated, data-rich platforms. A major opportunity lies in multiplexed liquid-biopsy analysis, where exosomes, circulating tumor nucleic acids, proteins, and metabolites can be interrogated in parallel to improve diagnostic robustness and longitudinal monitoring. Electrochemical transduction is particularly attractive for such multimodal formats because it is inherently low-power, miniaturizable, and compatible with microfluidic automation and point-of-care instrumentation ref [201], ref [202].

Another important direction is the convergence of nanomaterials, CRISPR-enabled recognition, and wearable or flexible electronics. CRISPR-based electrochemical biosensors have demonstrated ultralow detection limits and programmable specificity for nucleic-acid biomarkers, suggesting a path toward rapid mutation-resolved cancer testing outside centralized laboratories ref [203], ref [204]. In parallel, wearable electrochemical systems and soft bioelectronic interfaces are expanding continuous or near-continuous monitoring concepts from metabolites toward disease-relevant protein and nucleic-acid targets, although biofouling control and calibration stability remain central challenges ref [205], ref [206].

Future progress will also depend on digitalization. Machine-learning-assisted interpretation of multivariate electrochemical signals could help distinguish weak biomarker signatures from matrix effects and patient heterogeneity, especially in multiplex settings ref [207]. At the device level, additive manufacturing and paper or polymer-based fabrication may accelerate low-cost prototyping and decentralized production, but future studies must pair these innovations with rigorous clinical validation, interoperable data standards, and prospective trials to demonstrate utility in real oncology workflows ref [208].
